title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking every seen value in a set versus a simple adjacent-node comparison exploiting the sorted guarantee.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the head of a SORTED linked list, delete all duplicate values such that each distinct value appears only once, and return the resulting (still sorted) linked list.

blocks.caption: A duplicate must sit immediately next to its match in a sorted list, so only adjacent comparisons are needed

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a linked list, already sorted in non-decreasing order"],["Output","The same list, modified in place, with every duplicate value removed except its first occurrence"],["Goal","Remove duplicates in a single pass, exploiting the sorted structure"],["Constraints","The number of nodes is in the range [0, 300]; -100 <= Node.val <= 100; the list is guaranteed sorted in non-decreasing order"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The list is ALREADY SORTED","Any duplicate values must sit immediately ADJACENT to each other, so only neighboring nodes ever need to be compared"],["Removing a duplicate means skipping over a node entirely","Adjust the current node's next pointer to skip past the duplicate, without needing a separate \"previous\" pointer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a sorted linked list, remove every duplicate occurrence of a value, keeping only its first appearance, and return the resulting list.

blocks.title: Analogy: Skipping Repeated Entries in an Alphabetized Sign-In Sheet
blocks.text: Like reading through an alphabetized sign-in sheet where the same name might appear several times in a row (since the sheet is sorted), and crossing out every repeat entry immediately after the first one for that name. Because the sheet is sorted, repeats of the same name are guaranteed to be consecutive, so only ever needing to glance at the very next line to check for a repeat is enough.

blocks.caption: Since the list is sorted, a repeated value can only ever be the very next node

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: head = [1,1,2,3,3]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The first 1 and second 1 are adjacent; skip the second. The values 2, then 3, are next; the first 3 and second 3 are adjacent; skip the second","Kept values: 1, 2, 3","Every duplicate was immediately adjacent to its match, exactly as guaranteed by the sorted order"],["Answer","[1,2,3]","Each distinct value now appears exactly once"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: head is empty or has no duplicates at all
An empty list, or a list with no repeated values, is returned completely unchanged, since there's nothing to remove.
5. How Should We Think?
Before tracking every value seen so far in a set (which would work for ANY list, sorted or not), notice that the SORTED guarantee means duplicates can only ever be immediately adjacent.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In a sorted list, if a value repeats, every occurrence of it must appear consecutively, one right after another, since the list never "jumps back" to a smaller value.

Observation 2: This means checking whether the CURRENT node's value equals its IMMEDIATE next node's value is sufficient to detect every duplicate; there's no need to remember anything from further back in the list.

Observation 3: When a duplicate is found, the current node's next pointer can simply be redirected to skip over the duplicate node entirely (pointing to whatever came after it instead), effectively removing it from the list.

Observation 4: The current pointer should only advance forward once a genuinely NEW (non-duplicate) value has been confirmed; when a duplicate is skipped, the current pointer stays put, since the node now immediately following it might ALSO be a duplicate of the same value.

Recognizing that "sorted" specifically means "duplicates are always adjacent" is what allows a simple single-pointer, single-pass comparison to replace the need for tracking a whole set of previously-seen values.
This is a direct exploitation of the sorted-list guarantee: only ever comparing a node to its immediate neighbor is sufficient to catch every duplicate.
6. Brute Force Solution
Track every value seen so far in a set, removing any node whose value has already been recorded, regardless of position.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk through the list, maintaining a set of every value already seen.
For each node, if its value is already in the set, remove it (redirect the previous node's next pointer to skip it); otherwise, record its value and advance normally.

codes.python:
def delete_duplicates(head):
    seen = set()
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    node = head
    while node:
        if node.val in seen:                                                # this value has already appeared somewhere earlier
            prev.next = node.next                                          # skip this duplicate node entirely
        else:
            seen.add(node.val)
            prev = node
        node = node.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(3)))))
    result = delete_duplicates(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A dummy head simplifies the logic for potentially removing the very first node (though in a sorted list with duplicates, the very first value is always kept, since it's the first occurrence).
The set works correctly for ANY list (sorted or not), since it directly tracks every value already seen, regardless of position.
prev tracks the last confirmed non-duplicate node, so its next pointer can be adjusted correctly whenever a later duplicate is skipped.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every duplicate value, wherever it appears, is correctly identified and removed, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(n) in the worst case, for the set of seen values (though bounded by the value range, since values are only -100 to 100 here).

Limitation: tracking every previously-seen value in a set works for an unsorted list too, but ignores that the SORTED guarantee here means a much simpler O(1)-space check (comparing only to the immediate next node) is sufficient.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force tracks every value seen anywhere in the list. Instead, exploit the sorted guarantee: maintain a single curr pointer, and at each step, compare curr's value to curr.next's value. If they match, skip curr.next entirely by redirecting curr.next to curr.next.next (without advancing curr, since the newly-skipped-to node might ALSO match). If they don't match, advance curr normally to curr.next.

Maintain curr, starting at head. While curr and curr.next both exist: if curr.val equals curr.next.val, set curr.next = curr.next.next (skip the duplicate, without moving curr forward). Otherwise, advance curr to curr.next. Return head once the loop ends.
9. Optimized Solution
Compare each node only to its immediate next node, skipping duplicates directly without needing to track a set of seen values.
Dry run for head = [1,1,2,3,3]

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: curr.next becomes null, ending the loop, leaving the list as [1,2,3], matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the single curr pointer.
Why This Works

Because the list is sorted, any two nodes sharing the same value must be adjacent to each other (nothing smaller or different can appear between two equal values in sorted order). Checking curr against curr.next therefore catches every duplicate without missing any, and skipping curr.next by redirecting curr's pointer removes it directly. Not advancing curr after a skip correctly handles runs of MORE than 2 duplicate values in a row, since curr must keep re-checking against whatever new node now immediately follows it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["curr.val == curr.next.val","Skip curr.next directly (curr.next = curr.next.next); curr stays in place to re-check the new next node"],["curr.val != curr.next.val","Advance curr forward to curr.next, since the current value has no more duplicates left"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: No dummy head is needed here, since a sorted list's very first value is always kept (it's the first occurrence of whatever that value is).
curr only ever advances when a confirmed non-duplicate transition is found, correctly handling arbitrarily long runs of the same repeated value.
The loop condition (curr && curr.next) naturally stops once curr reaches the last node, with nothing left to compare against.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (track every seen value in a set)","O(n)","O(n) (or bounded by value range)","Works for any list, sorted or not, but doesn't exploit the sorted guarantee"],["Optimized (compare only to the immediate next node)","O(n)","O(1) extra","Exploits the sorted guarantee directly, needing no extra tracking structure at all"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a sequence is guaranteed sorted, duplicate detection collapses to a simple adjacent-comparison, since equal values can never be separated by anything else, eliminating the need for any extra tracking structure.
Common mistakes

items: Advancing curr forward even after skipping a duplicate, which can miss additional duplicates in a run of 3 or more identical values.
Forgetting the loop's bounds check on curr.next, risking a null pointer dereference when curr is the last node.
Using the more general set-tracking approach out of habit, missing the opportunity to exploit the sorted guarantee for a simpler, more space-efficient solution.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly state why the sorted guarantee reduces this to an adjacent-only comparison, since recognizing and exploiting problem-specific structure (rather than defaulting to a general-purpose technique) is exactly what distinguishes a strong answer here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove duplicates from a SORTED sequence" points toward comparing only adjacent elements, since sorting guarantees duplicates must be neighbors, needing no extra tracking structure.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if the list were NOT sorted? Duplicates could appear anywhere relative to each other, requiring the more general set-based tracking approach (the brute force shown here) instead.

How would you remove duplicates but delete ALL occurrences of any value that repeats (keeping none of them)? This becomes Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II, requiring a dummy head and more careful boundary tracking, since the very first node might itself need removing.
How would you count how many duplicates were removed? Add a simple counter, incremented each time the skip branch executes.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct precursor to Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II elsewhere in this category, which extends this exact adjacent-comparison idea to remove ALL occurrences of any repeated value instead of keeping the first.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (adjacent-only comparison): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Adjacent-node comparison, exploiting the sorted-list guarantee
Core Idea: In a sorted list, duplicates must be immediately adjacent; skip curr.next directly on a match, without advancing curr
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A sorted sequence guarantees duplicates are always neighbors, eliminating the need for any extra tracking structure
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: If curr.val == curr.next.val, skip curr.next; otherwise advance curr
